# Rust vs. Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report compares Rust and Go for network services, focusing on performance and developer productivity.

## Performance

### Latency
*   Go generally exhibits lower P50-P95 latency [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   Go also tends to have better P99 tail latency in various benchmarks [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
*   Rust can achieve significantly improved P50 latency with optimization, such as eliminating per-request allocations [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   Rust offers ultra-low, garbage collection (GC)-free tail latencies and predictable performance, making it suitable for latency-critical applications [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).

### Throughput
*   In one benchmark, Rust initially showed higher throughput than Go (13.2M vs. 9.5M) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   After optimization, Rust's throughput nearly matched Go's (28.8M vs. 28.6M), representing a 74% increase for Rust [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   In a Raspberry Pi 5 benchmark, Go, .NET, and Node.js generally outpaced Rust in raw weighted throughput (around 2,200-2,461 req/s vs. 2,125 req/s for Rust) [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932).
*   For a high-throughput HTTP server sorting values, Go consistently outperformed Rust across various request and array sizes [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).

### Memory Efficiency
*   Rust can be substantially more memory-efficient than Go, using about 57% less memory in optimized scenarios (224 MB vs. 521 MB) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   Rust typically has a lower RAM footprint (7.36 MB in one test), remaining flat with no GC events, while Go shows visible GC pauses but stays under 20 MB [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932).
*   Rust achieves the best efficiency in terms of throughput per RAM, being approximately 2.8 times faster per RAM than Go (310.25 req/s/MB for Rust) [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932).
*   Rust's ownership model allows for deterministic memory usage and zero GC pauses [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
*   Go's garbage collector can introduce occasional pauses and a higher memory footprint under heavy heap usage [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).

### Concurrency and Reliability
*   Both Rust and Go exhibit very low error rates in performance tests [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   In one test, Go had zero failures, while Rust had a small number (516, or 0.002%) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
*   On a Raspberry Pi 5, both Rust and Go plateaued near 14k-17k requests per second at a concurrency of around 120 [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932).
*   Go utilizes goroutines for concurrency, offering an easy approach [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
*   Rust relies on ownership guarantees for "fearless concurrency" [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).

## Developer Productivity

### Learning Curve
*   Go has a lower, gentler learning curve, making it easier for developers to onboard quickly [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
*   Rust has a steeper learning curve due to concepts like ownership, lifetimes, Send/Sync, and its lack of a garbage collector [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).

### Development Speed
*   Go emphasizes rapid development with fast build times and readable code [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
*   Rust typically has slower build times, especially for larger codebases, due to its ownership model and complex compilation [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
*   Go is well-suited for quick-delivery backend services and offers high developer velocity [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).

### Ecosystem and Tooling
*   Go has a strong ecosystem for cloud and networking, including a convenient standard library (`net/http`) [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/) [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
*   Rust's tooling for HTTP servers can be more fragmented [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).

### Use Cases and Suitability
*   **Go is generally chosen for**:
    *   Rapid feature iteration, cloud-native APIs, data ingestion pipelines, and standard CRUD microservices [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).
    *   Backend services, network/I/O bound workloads, and cloud tooling where developer velocity is crucial [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
    *   Maintaining code and teams needing fast builds [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
*   **Rust is generally chosen for**:
    *   Performance-critical, low-latency, and memory-safety-required code [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
    *   Systems programming, embedded work, and WebAssembly [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [techloghub.com](https://techloghub.com/compare/go-vs-rust).
    *   Core cloud infrastructure, networking proxies, distributed storage, cryptography, and real-time streaming where every millisecond and memory byte matters [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).

### Mixed Approach
*   Many teams adopt a mixed approach, using Go for most business services and Rust for specific high-performance or safety-critical components [nexzem.com](https://nexzem.com/compare/go-vs-rust) [oscave.com](https://oscave.com/blog/rust-vs-go-for-microservices-architecture-trade-offs).

## Rust vs. Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report summarizes the trade-offs between Rust and Go for network services, focusing on performance and developer productivity.

### Performance

*   **General Performance Characteristics**
    *   Go generally offers lower latency at common percentiles and more consistent tail latency [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   Rust can achieve comparable throughput to Go [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   Rust can beat Go on median latency when heap allocations are removed from the hot path [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   Rust generally uses less memory than Go [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   Go utilizes a garbage collector (GC), while Rust does not, leading to more predictable latency in Rust [rustify.rs](https://rustify.rs/articles/rust-vs-go-backend-2026) [devtoolswatch.com](https://devtoolswatch.com/en/rust-vs-go-backend-2026).
    *   Rust guarantees memory safety at compile-time, whereas Go relies on runtime checks [rustify.rs](https://rustify.rs/articles/rust-vs-go-backend-2026).

*   **Specific Benchmark Results**
    *   In a high-throughput HTTP server benchmark involving `O(n log n)` sorting per request, Go consistently outperformed Rust in both average and maximum total and server-side sorting times across various data sizes (1,000, 10,000, and 100,000 items) [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
        *   For 1,000 items, Go server averaged ~0.12 ms for sorting and ~1.04 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~0.43 ms for sorting and ~1.99 ms roundtrip [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
        *   For 10,000 items, Go server averaged ~0.96 ms for sorting and ~8.37 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~4.11 ms for sorting and ~15.44 ms roundtrip [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
        *   For 100,000 items, Go server averaged ~6.85 ms for sorting and ~59.84 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~34.32 ms for sorting and ~139.93 ms roundtrip [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
    *   In a benchmark comparing HTTP servers performing 100 SHA256 iterations per request under Kubernetes load:
        *   Initially, Go was faster on most latency metrics (P50, P90, P95) and had higher overall throughput [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
        *   With more resources, Go outperformed Rust in latency and throughput (Go ~21.8M total requests vs. Rust ~16.5M) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
        *   After Rust optimizations (eliminating `Vec` allocations, using fixed-size arrays), Rust achieved a P50 latency win (0.203 ms vs Go 0.255 ms) and nearly identical throughput to Go (Rust 28.8M vs Go 28.6–28.8M) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
        *   Rust used substantially less memory (~224 MB vs Go ~521 MB) but had higher CPU usage in the optimized scenario [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
        *   Go maintained better tail latency (P99) and had zero failures, while Rust had a small number of timeouts (0.002%) [github.com](https://github.com/huseyinbabal/benchmarks/tree/main/rust-server-vs-goserver).
    *   In a benchmark of self-hosted CRUD APIs over SQLite on a Raspberry Pi 5, Rust showed the highest throughput-to-RAM efficiency at 310.25 req/s/MB (read-heavy mix), approximately 2.8 times higher than Go [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932). Rust also had the lowest weighted peak RAM usage at 7.36 MB [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932). Go plateaued around c=120 in concurrency scaling [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.11932).

### Developer Productivity

*   **Learning Curve and Onboarding**
    *   Go has a faster learning curve and offers quicker onboarding (2–4 weeks) [rustify.rs](https://rustify.rs/articles/rust-vs-go-backend-2026).
    *   Rust requires a greater learning investment, with ramp-up times of 4–6 months for specialization [rustify.rs](https://rustify.rs/articles/rust-vs-go-backend-2026) [devtoolswatch.com](https://devtoolswatch.com/en/rust-vs-go-backend-2026).

*   **Ecosystem and Tooling**
    *   Go's standard library (`net/http`) is considered easier and more convenient for HTTP APIs [jmkopper.github.io](https://jmkopper.github.io/posts/2023/04/go-rust/).
    *   Go has a mature and robust ecosystem for cloud-native development and Kubernetes [rustify.rs](https://rustify.rs/articles/rust-vs-go-backend-2026).

## Rust vs. Go for Network Services: Performance and Developer Productivity Trade-offs

This report summarizes the trade-offs between Rust and Go for network services, focusing on performance and developer productivity.

### Performance

*   **General Performance Characteristics**
    *   Go generally offers lower latency at common percentiles and more consistent tail latency [S2].
    *   Rust can achieve comparable throughput to Go [S2].
    *   Rust can beat Go on median latency when heap allocations are removed from the hot path [S2].
    *   Rust generally uses less memory than Go [S2].
    *   Go utilizes a garbage collector (GC), while Rust does not, leading to more predictable latency in Rust [S4][S5].
    *   Rust guarantees memory safety at compile-time, whereas Go relies on runtime checks [S4].

*   **Specific Benchmark Results**
    *   In a high-throughput HTTP server benchmark involving `O(n log n)` sorting per request, Go consistently outperformed Rust in both average and maximum total and server-side sorting times across various data sizes (1,000, 10,000, and 100,000 items) [S1].
        *   For 1,000 items, Go server averaged ~0.12 ms for sorting and ~1.04 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~0.43 ms for sorting and ~1.99 ms roundtrip [S1].
        *   For 10,000 items, Go server averaged ~0.96 ms for sorting and ~8.37 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~4.11 ms for sorting and ~15.44 ms roundtrip [S1].
        *   For 100,000 items, Go server averaged ~6.85 ms for sorting and ~59.84 ms roundtrip, while Rust averaged ~34.32 ms for sorting and ~139.93 ms roundtrip [S1].
    *   In a benchmark comparing HTTP servers performing 100 SHA256 iterations per request under Kubernetes load:
        *   Initially, Go was faster on most latency metrics (P50, P90, P95) and had higher overall throughput [S2].
        *   With more resources, Go outperformed Rust in latency and throughput (Go ~21.8M total requests vs. Rust ~16.5M) [S2].
        *   After Rust optimizations (eliminating `Vec` allocations, using fixed-size arrays), Rust achieved a P50 latency win (0.203 ms vs Go 0.255 ms) and nearly identical throughput to Go (Rust 28.8M vs Go 28.6–28.8M) [S2].
        *   Rust used substantially less memory (~224 MB vs Go ~521 MB) but had higher CPU usage in the optimized scenario [S2].
        *   Go maintained better tail latency (P99) and had zero failures, while Rust had a small number of timeouts (0.002%) [S2].
    *   In a benchmark of self-hosted CRUD APIs over SQLite on a Raspberry Pi 5, Rust showed the highest throughput-to-RAM efficiency at 310.25 req/s/MB (read-heavy mix), approximately 2.8 times higher than Go [S3]. Rust also had the lowest weighted peak RAM usage at 7.36 MB [S3]. Go plateaued around c=120 in concurrency scaling [S3].

### Developer Productivity

*   **Learning Curve and Onboarding**
    *   Go has a faster learning curve and offers quicker onboarding (2–4 weeks) [S4].
    *   Rust requires a greater learning investment, with ramp-up times of 4–6 months for specialization [S4][S5].

*   **Ecosystem and Tooling**
    *   Go's standard library (`net/http`) is considered easier and more convenient for HTTP APIs [S1].
    *   Go has a mature and robust ecosystem for cloud-native development and Kubernetes [S4].
    *   Rust often requires third-party crates for functionalities like HTTP and environment loading, which can add complexity [S1].
    *   Rust's ecosystem is strong for infrastructure, AI infrastructure, WebAssembly (Wasm), and systems programming [S4].

*   **Concurrency Model**
    *   Go offers simple concurrency through goroutines [S4].
    *   Rust has an explicit async model [S4].

*   **Development Philosophy**
    *   Go is often chosen for speed to market, large-scale team onboarding, standard microservices (REST/gRPC, CRUD), and minimizing development cost [S5]. It's considered a pragmatic default for most teams, offering 80% of performance at approximately 20% of the development cost [S5].
    *   Rust is preferred when performance, memory efficiency, or safety are non-negotiable [S5]. It's ideal for foundational/infrastructure workloads such as proxies, embedded runtimes, and WebAssembly [S5].

*   **Job Market and Salary (2026 Outlook)**
    *   Go has a large job market with broad backend and cloud-native opportunities; senior USA salaries are roughly $165K–$205K [S4].
    *   Rust has a smaller but growing job market, targeting scarcer, higher-upside roles in infrastructure and performance-critical backend work; senior USA salaries are roughly $185K–$230K [S4]. Top startup pay can be around $192K [S4].
    *   Finding engineers for niche stacks like Rust and Go often requires targeting open-source activity on platforms like GitHub rather than traditional job boards [S6].

*   **Hybrid Approach**
    *   Many organizations use both languages, employing Go for most microservices and Rust for performance-critical components (e.g., real-time processing, custom proxies, data pipelines) [S5]. Companies like Dropbox, Discord, and Cloudflare utilize this hybrid strategy [S5].

Summary:
- Purpose: Compare Go and Rust performance for a high-throughput HTTP server performing O(n log n) sorting per request.
- Setup: JSON input with a secret, budget, and a list of tests; server sorts tests by value and returns those below the budget. Three test Scenarios with varying request counts and data sizes to separate transmission, data handling, and algorithm time.
- Key results (avg times):
  - 1,000 items: Go server ~0.12 ms (sorting) / ~1.04 ms roundtrip; Rust server ~0.43 ms (sorting) / ~1.99 ms roundtrip.
  - 10,000 items: Go server ~0.96 ms (sorting) / ~8.37 ms roundtrip; Rust server ~4.11 ms (sorting) / ~15.44 ms roundtrip.
  - 100,000 items: Go server ~6.85 ms (sorting) / ~59.84 ms roundtrip; Rust server ~34.32 ms (sorting) / ~139.93 ms roundtrip.
- Max times (similar trend):
  - 1,000 items: Go ~0.72 ms / 2.77 ms; Rust ~1.47 ms / 5.35 ms.
  - 10,000 items: Go ~2.71 ms / 15.84 ms; Rust ~11.27 ms / 34.67 ms.
  - 100,000 items: Go ~9.38 ms / 66.54 ms; Rust ~46.69 ms / 176.14 ms.
- Editor’s note: The author observed Go outperforming Rust in these tests and questions why Rust underperformed; provides subjective experiences and code-size comparisons (Go server ~94 lines, Rust server ~65 lines, with a Go 5-second timeout accounted for in the Go code).
- Additional observations:
  - Go’s standard library (net/http) is easier and more convenient for HTTP APIs.
  - Rust requires third-party crates for HTTP and environment loading (.env), contributing to complexity.
- Bottom line: In this particular setup and workloads, Go outperformed Rust in both average and max total and server-side sorting times, though the author notes uncertainty about the Rust underperformance. The study emphasizes that the Go ecosystem’s standard tooling contributes to easier development and potentially faster results in this benchmark.

Here are the essential results from the Rust vs Go comparison for a CPU-bound microservice with a p99 SLO of 15 ms:

- Throughput at p99 < 15 ms (max requests per second):
  - Rust (axum): 9,840 rps
  - Go (net/http): 7,410 rps
  - With Go tuning: 8,120–8,560 rps depending on GC settings

- Latency (p99 at the rate that stays under p99 < 15 ms):
  - Rust: 14.6 ms
  - Go (default): 14.8 ms
  - Go with GC tuning: around 14.9 ms (GOMEMLIMIT if memory-constrained)

- Tail latency (p99.9 at that rate):
  - Rust: 22.9 ms
  - Go (default): 48.3 ms
  - Go with memory limit / tuned GC: 33.6–39.1 ms

- Memory / RSS (same rate):
  - Rust: ~41 MB
  - Go (default): ~131 MB
  - Go with GC tuning (high memory): 346 MB to 782 MB depending on settings

- Relative efficiency:
  - Rust sustains ~33% more throughput per box than default Go
  - Go GC behavior introduces tail latency due to stalls; tuning can reduce tail latency but increases memory usage

- Practical recommendations:
  - If CPU-bound with strict p99 SLO and you can use Rust: Rust is preferred for better throughput and lower tail latency with far less memory.
  - If you must stay with Go: use GOMEMLIMIT (and possibly other GC tuning) to stay under SLO with a reasonable acceptance of higher CPU usage; avoid rewriting unless tail latency is the primary blocker.
  - Don’t rewrite Go for median gains; focus on tail latency improvements with GC tuning first.

- Additional notes:
  - The observed differences in tail latency are largely due to Go’s garbage collection pauses versus Rust’s deterministic memory management.
  - Fixed-rate load tests (wrk2) reveal tail behavior more reliably than traditional wrk, which can mask tail latency.

Essential results from "Go vs Rust for backend services at scale: what real teams chose" (How They Scaled):

- Verdict: Both languages appear in successful, real-world systems; Rust is favored where teams hit garbage-collection pauses or need lower latency and memory efficiency, while Go is used in many scalable systems that perform fine. No clear winner; choice depends on workload.

- Key patterns:
  - Rust: chosen to reduce GC latency and improve performance in high-load, memory-sensitive components (e.g., Discord Read States, Cloudflare Pingora, Figma, Datadog’s timing/indexing enhancements).
  - Go: widely used in scalable services where GC is acceptable or manageable, and for general-purpose backend workloads (e.g., Cloudflare Quicksilver, Slack’s Flannel).

- Notable "direct comparison" story:
  - Discord rewrote its Read States service from Go to Rust to eliminate GC latency spikes in a large in-memory cache.

- Representative scale figures from the stories:
  - Rust-focused cases: 70M+ requests/sec (OpenAI case cited), hundreds of database nodes (Discord), 178.6B rows/sec (Axiom).
  - Go-focused cases: multi-tenant and caching-heavy systems; Cloudflare and Slack examples show large-scale deployments with Go.

- Examples of stacks and use cases:
  - Rust: rewrites for latency-critical components, high-throughput indexing, distributed storage layering, and edge proxy infrastructure (Pingora).
  - Go: edge services, analytics pipelines, and general backend services that scaled well without forcing a language switch.

- Scope of data:
  - 7 Go stories vs. 10 Rust stories in the database; companies span Cloudflare, Datadog, Discord, Dropbox, Slack (Go) and OpenAI, Figma, Axiom (Rust) among others.

In short: Go remains viable for large-scale backends; Rust is favored when minimizing GC impact and achieving low latency/memory footprint is critical. The decision should be guided by the specific system requirements rather than a universal “winner.”

Summary:
- FrontierRefactor introduces a 60-task benchmark spanning four scales (kernels to full repos) to evaluate multi-scale, performance-oriented codebase refactoring while preserving externally observable behavior.
- Key finding: functional correctness does not guarantee performance improvements. Across 1,080 execution runs, only 41.2% of functionally equivalent submissions produced verified speedups; 19.3% had active performance regressions and 21.9% were obscured by measurement noise.
- Refactoring paradigms show orthogonal bottlenecks:
  - In-place optimizations reliably preserve contracts (86.5% pass) but seldom achieve acceleration without profiling.
  - Cross-language rewrites can yield substantial speedups when compiled but exhibit contract fragility (module pass 65.0% drops to 32.6% at package scale).
- Trajectory audits reveal a profiling blind spot: agents often optimize for syntactic readability rather than empirical cost. Introducing multi-turn timing feedback improves strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%.
- Performance outcomes vary by model/harness:
  - Across evaluation suites including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and DeepSeek, a majority of behavior-preserving submissions fail the performance gate (e.g., Claude Opus 5: 56.3% fail; GPT-5.6 Sol: 63.5% fail).
- Overall takeaway: behavioral preservation and physical acceleration are decoupled; achieving reliable speedups requires explicit performance profiling and feedback during multi-turn refactoring, and there is a notable gap between passing functional checks and verifiable performance gains.

*   **Throughput**
    *   Rust generally achieves higher throughput for CPU-bound microservices and concurrent TCP servers [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/) [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   For a CPU-bound microservice with a p99 SLO of 15ms, Rust (axum) achieved 9,840 requests per second (rps) compared to Go (net/http) at 7,410 rps (default) or 8,120–8,560 rps (tuned) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/). Rust sustained approximately 33% more throughput per box than default Go [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   In a benchmark of concurrent TCP servers on a 128-core AMD EPYC server, Rust 1.85 achieved 14.2 million RPS, while Go 1.24 achieved 11.8 million RPS, indicating Rust was approximately 20% higher [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).
    *   In JSON benchmarks for production-grade microservices, Rust achieved approximately 1.423 million requests/second compared to Go's 620,000 requests/second [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **Latency**
    *   Rust generally demonstrates lower tail latency (p99 and p99.9) due to its deterministic memory management, while Go's garbage collection (GC) can introduce pauses and higher tail latencies [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/) [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).
    *   For a CPU-bound microservice under a p99 < 15ms SLO, Rust had a p99 latency of 14.6ms, while Go (default) had 14.8ms. At p99.9, Rust was 22.9ms compared to Go's 48.3ms (default) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   At a rate of 4,000 requests/second, Rust was approximately twice as fast at p99 (6.8ms vs 12.7ms) and 2.8 times faster at p99.9 (11.2ms vs 31.4ms) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   In a concurrent TCP server benchmark, Rust 1.85 had a 99th percentile latency of 82 μs, whereas Go 1.24 had 117 μs [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).
    *   For JSON echo at 10,000 connections, Rust achieved a p99 latency of approximately 0.8ms, while Go was around 1.9ms [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Go's GC pauses occur approximately every 40ms and significantly affect tail latency, while Rust's deterministic memory management avoids these periodic stalls [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Tuning Go's GC (e.g., with GOMEMLIMIT) can reduce tail latency but often at the cost of increased memory usage [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).

*   **Memory Usage**
    *   Rust typically uses significantly less memory than Go [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   For a CPU-bound microservice, Rust consumed approximately 41 MB of RSS at maximum throughput, compared to Go's 131 MB (default) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/). Go can use 2.9 times more memory than Rust at 4,000 requests/second [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   With GC tuning, Go's memory usage can increase substantially (e.g., 346 MB to 782 MB) [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   In JSON benchmarks, Rust used approximately 18 MB RSS at 10,000 connections, while Go used around 30 MB [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   For concurrent TCP servers, Go 1.24 has approximately 4 μs GC pauses for 10 GB heaps, while Rust has no GC but uses approximately 18% more memory in this specific benchmark [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).

*   **CPU Usage**
    *   Rust generally uses less CPU than Go for similar workloads [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   At 4,000 requests/second, Rust used 61% CPU compared to Go's 78%, meaning Go used about 17% more CPU [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rust sustains approximately 33% more requests per vCPU-second than Go [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).

*   **Cold Start & Binary Size**
    *   Go generally has faster cold start times [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need). Rust's cold start was ~11 ms compared to Go's ~4 ms [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Rust typically produces smaller binaries. Rust binaries are around 3.2 MB (static), while Go binaries range from 8–14 MB depending on static or dynamic linking [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

### Developer Productivity

*   **Learning Curve & Development Speed**
    *   Go has a significantly easier and faster learning curve than Rust [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Go's learning curve is rated 3/10, while Rust's is 7/10 [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).
    *   It takes approximately 2–3 weeks to become productive with Go, compared to 8–12 weeks for Rust [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Go offers faster initial deployment; a "Hello World" TCP server can be deployed in 12 seconds with Go versus 47 seconds with Rust [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput).
    *   Go generally allows for faster developer velocity. One team shipped 12 endpoints in 6 weeks with Go, while a Rust team shipped 7 endpoints in the same period [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **Build Times**
    *   Go has faster incremental build times. Rust full builds can take approximately 48 seconds (release), while Go incremental builds are around 3.2 seconds [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **Concurrency Model**
    *   Go uses goroutines for concurrency, while Rust uses async/await with Tokio [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **Memory Management**
    *   Rust uses an ownership model with no garbage collector (GC), leading to deterministic memory management [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Go uses a concurrent tri-color garbage collector [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **Security Tooling**
    *   Rust uses `crates.io/cargo-audit` for security, while Go uses `proxy.golang.io/govulncheck` [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

### Practical Considerations and Trade-offs

*   **When to Choose Rust**
    *   Rust is preferred for CPU-bound, latency-critical hot paths with strict p99/p99.9 SLOs that require better throughput, lower tail latency, and significantly less memory [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/) [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need) [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   It's chosen to reduce GC latency and improve performance in high-load, memory-sensitive components [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   Examples include rewriting services to eliminate GC latency spikes in large in-memory caches (e.g., Discord Read States) and for edge proxy infrastructure [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   Rust can save on compute costs, with one estimate showing savings of approximately $2,400/month on AWS Graviton3 for 100 million daily requests compared to Go [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **When to Choose Go**
    *   Go is suitable when developer velocity, ease of deployment, faster time-to-production, and simpler maintenance are priorities, especially when throughput needs are lower or acceptable with GC [johal.in](https://johal.in/benchmark-go-124-vs-rust-185-concurrent-tcp-throughput) [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need) [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   It excels in rapid iteration and familiarity [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).
    *   Go is widely used in scalable services where GC is acceptable or manageable and for general-purpose backend workloads [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   If a Go team has headroom in their SLOs, Go with GOMEMLIMIT can achieve similar SLOs but will use more CPU and memory [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).
    *   Rewriting a Go service solely for median performance gains (p50) is often not recommended; focus on tail latency improvements (GC tuning, allocations) first [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).

*   **Hybrid Approach**
    *   A hybrid approach is often effective: use Go for greenfield features and general-purpose services, and Rust for performance-critical hot paths requiring low latency and high throughput [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need) [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   Replacing hot-path components with Rust can dramatically reduce p99 latency and compute costs while keeping non-critical layers in Go [johal.in](https://johal.in/performance-battle-cloud-vs-go-what-you-need).

*   **General Guidance**
    *   The choice between Rust and Go depends heavily on specific system requirements and workload characteristics [howtheyscaled.com](https://howtheyscaled.com/compare/go-vs-rust/).
    *   Behavioral preservation does not guarantee performance improvements, and achieving reliable speedups requires explicit performance profiling and feedback during refactoring [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.25834).
    *   Use fixed-rate load testing (e.g., `wrk2`) to accurately reveal true tail latency behavior, as closed-loop tests can be misleading [blogs.lamplitlabs.com](https://blogs.lamplitlabs.com/posts/rust-vs-go-cpu-bound-microservice/).

Essential results from "Go vs Rust for backend services at scale: what real teams chose" (How They Scaled):

- Verdict: Both languages appear in successful, real-world systems; Rust is favored where teams hit garbage-collection pauses or need lower latency and memory efficiency, while Go is used in many scalable systems that perform fine. No clear winner; choice depends on workload.

- Key patterns:
  - Rust: chosen to reduce GC latency and improve performance in high-load, memory-sensitive components (e.g., Discord Read States, Cloudflare Pingora, Figma, Datadog’s timing/indexing enhancements).
  - Go: widely used in scalable services where GC is acceptable or manageable, and for general-purpose backend workloads (e.g., Cloudflare Quicksilver, Slack’s Flannel).

- Notable "direct comparison" story:
  - Discord rewrote its Read States service from Go to Rust to eliminate GC latency spikes in a large in-memory cache.

- Representative scale figures from the stories:
  - Rust-focused cases: 70M+ requests/sec (OpenAI case cited), hundreds of database nodes (Discord), 178.6B rows/sec (Axiom).
  - Go-focused cases: multi-tenant and caching-heavy systems; Cloudflare and Slack examples show large-scale deployments with Go.

- Examples of stacks and use cases:
  - Rust: rewrites for latency-critical components, high-throughput indexing, distributed storage layering, and edge proxy infrastructure (Pingora).
  - Go: edge services, analytics pipelines, and general backend services that scaled well without forcing a language switch.

- Scope of data:
  - 7 Go stories vs. 10 Rust stories in the database; companies span Cloudflare, Datadog, Discord, Dropbox, Slack (Go) and OpenAI, Figma, Axiom (Rust) among others.

In short: Go remains viable for large-scale backends; Rust is favored when minimizing GC impact and achieving low latency/memory footprint is critical. The decision should be guided by the specific system requirements rather than a universal “winner.”

Here are the essential results from the Rust vs Go comparison for a CPU-bound microservice with a p99 SLO of 15 ms:

- Throughput at p99 < 15 ms (max requests per second):
  - Rust (axum): 9,840 rps
  - Go (net/http): 7,410 rps
  - With Go tuning: 8,120–8,560 rps depending on GC settings

- Latency (p99 at the rate that stays under p99 < 15 ms):
  - Rust: 14.6 ms
  - Go (default): 14.8 ms
  - Go with GC tuning: around 14.9 ms (GOMEMLIMIT if memory-constrained)

- Tail latency (p99.9 at that rate):
  - Rust: 22.9 ms
  - Go (default): 48.3 ms
  - Go with memory limit / tuned GC: 33.6–39.1 ms

- Memory / RSS (same rate):
  - Rust: ~41 MB
  - Go (default): ~131 MB
  - Go with GC tuning (high memory): 346 MB to 782 MB depending on settings

- Relative efficiency:
  - Rust sustains ~33% more throughput per box than default Go
  - Go GC behavior introduces tail latency due to stalls; tuning can reduce tail latency but increases memory usage

- Practical recommendations:
  - If CPU-bound with strict p99 SLO and you can use Rust: Rust is preferred for better throughput and lower tail latency with far less memory.
  - If you must stay with Go: use GOMEMLIMIT (and possibly other GC tuning) to stay under SLO with a reasonable acceptance of higher CPU usage; avoid rewriting unless tail latency is the primary blocker.
  - Don’t rewrite Go for median gains; focus on tail latency improvements with GC tuning first.

- Additional notes:
  - The observed differences in tail latency are largely due to Go’s garbage collection pauses versus Rust’s deterministic memory management.
  - Fixed-rate load tests (wrk2) reveal tail behavior more reliably than traditional wrk, which can mask tail latency.

Summary:

- The study compares Rust (axum) vs Go (net/http) for a CPU-bound microservice under SLO: p99 < 15 ms.
- At 4,000 req/s:
  - p50: Rust 2.1 ms vs Go 2.6 ms (Rust ~20% faster)
  - p90: Rust 3.4 ms vs Go 4.9 ms
  - p99: Rust 6.8 ms vs Go 12.7 ms (Rust ~2x faster)
  - p99.9: Rust 11.2 ms vs Go 31.4 ms (Rust ~2.8x faster)
  - CPU: Rust 61% vs Go 78% (Go uses ~17% more CPU)
  - RSS: Rust 38 MB vs Go 112 MB (Go ~2.9x more memory)
- Go tail latency is heavily affected by GC pauses (~every 40 ms), causing larger p99/p99.9 tails. Rust frees buffers deterministically with no periodic stalls.
- Maximum sustainable throughput (p99 < 15 ms):
  - Max req/s: Rust 9,840 vs Go 7,410 (default Go)
  - p99 at max rate: ~14.6 ms (Rust) vs ~14.8 ms (Go) 
  - p99.9 at max rate: Rust 22.9 ms vs Go 48.3 ms (Go GC impact)
  - RSS at max rate: Rust 41 MB vs Go 131 MB
  - Requests per vCPU-second: Rust 2,460 vs Go 1,850 (Rust ~33% more)
- Throughput improvements in Go via GC tuning (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT) reduce tail latency but increase memory usage; with tuned Go (GOMEMLIMIT and GC tweaks) you can clear the SLO around ~8,500 req/s per box, at higher memory cost.
- Practical guidance:
  - For CPU-bound hot paths with strict p99 SLOs: prefer Rust for better tail latency and lower memory.
  - For Go teams with headroom SLOs: Go with GOMEMLIMIT achieves similar SLOs but uses more CPU and memory.
  - Don’t rewrite a Go service just to improve p50; focus on tail improvements first (GC, allocations) before considering a rewrite.
  - Use fixed-rate load testing (wrk2) to reveal true tail behavior; closed-loop tests (wrk) can mislead.

Bottom line: Rust offers significantly better tail latency and lower memory for a CPU-bound path; Go can meet the SLO with GC tuning but pays in tail latency and memory.

- Throughput at p99 < 15 ms (max requests per second):
  - Rust (axum): 9,840 rps
  - Go (net/http): 7,410 rps

  - Rust: 14.6 ms
  - Go (default): 14.8 ms
  - Go with GC tuning: around 14.9 ms (GOMEMLIMIT if memory-constrained)

- Tail latency (p99.9 at that rate):
  - Rust: 22.9 ms
  - Go (default): 48.3 ms
  - Go with memory limit / tuned GC: 33.6–39.1 ms

- Memory / RSS (same rate):
  - Rust: ~41 MB
  - Go (default): ~131 MB
  - Go with GC tuning (high memory): 346 MB to 782 MB depending on settings

- Relative efficiency:
  - Rust sustains ~33% more throughput per box than default Go
  - Go GC behavior introduces tail latency due to stalls; tuning can reduce tail latency but increases memory usage

- Practical recommendations:
  - If CPU-bound with strict p99 SLO and you can use Rust: Rust is preferred for better throughput and lower tail latency with far less memory.
  - If you must stay with Go: use GOMEMLIMIT (and possibly other GC tuning) to stay under SLO with a reasonable acceptance of higher CPU usage; avoid rewriting unless tail latency is the primary blocker.
  - Don’t rewrite Go for median gains; focus on tail latency improvements with GC tuning first.

- Additional notes:
  - The observed differences in tail latency are largely due to Go’s garbage collection pauses versus Rust’s deterministic memory management.
  - Fixed-rate load tests (wrk2) reveal tail behavior more reliably than traditional wrk, which can mask tail latency.

Summary:

- The study compares Rust (axum) vs Go (net/http) for a CPU-bound microservice under SLO: p99 < 15 ms.
- At 4,000 req/s:
  - p50: Rust 2.1 ms vs Go 2.6 ms (Rust ~20% faster)
  - p90: Rust 3.4 ms vs Go 4.9 ms
  - p99: Rust 6.8 ms vs Go 12.7 ms (Rust ~2x faster)
  - p99.9: Rust 11.2 ms vs Go 31.4 ms (Rust ~2.8x faster)
  - CPU: Rust 61% vs Go 78% (Go uses ~17% more CPU)
  - RSS: Rust 38 MB vs Go 112 MB (Go ~2.9x more memory)
- Go tail latency is heavily affected by GC pauses (~every 40 ms), causing larger p99/p99.9 tails. Rust frees buffers deterministically with no periodic stalls.
- Maximum sustainable throughput (p99 < 15 ms):
  - Max req/s: Rust 9,840 vs Go 7,410 (default Go)
  - p99 at max rate: ~14.6 ms (Rust) vs ~14.8 ms (Go) 
  - p99.9 at max rate: Rust 22.9 ms vs Go 48.3 ms (Go GC impact)
  - RSS at max rate: Rust 41 MB vs Go 131 MB
  - Requests per vCPU-second: Rust 2,460 vs Go 1,850 (Rust ~33% more)
- Throughput improvements in Go via GC tuning (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT) reduce tail latency but increase memory usage; with tuned Go (GOMEMLIMIT and GC tweaks) you can clear the SLO around ~8,500 req/s per box, at higher memory cost.
- Practical guidance:
  - For CPU-bound hot paths with strict p99 SLOs: prefer Rust for better tail latency and lower memory.
  - For Go teams with headroom SLOs: Go with GOMEMLIMIT achieves similar SLOs but uses more CPU and memory.
  - Don’t rewrite a Go service just to improve p50; focus on tail improvements first (GC, allocations) before considering a rewrite.
  - Use fixed-rate load testing (wrk2) to reveal true tail behavior; closed-loop tests (wrk) can mislead.

Bottom line: Rust offers significantly better tail latency and lower memory for a CPU-bound path; Go can meet the SLO with GC tuning but pays in tail latency and memory.

Summary:
- This document is the 1.0 specification for a Raft-like consensus protocol implemented by raft-io. It defines the protocol’s state, messages, on-wire and on-disk formats, and the invariants the implementation guarantees.
- The API, message set, wire framing, durable WAL record format, and configuration encoding are frozen and backward-incompatible changes are not planned before 2.0. New message variants may be added, but existing ones remain fixed to preserve interoperability.
- Key concepts:
  - Cluster consists of nodes identified by NodeId (unsigned 64-bit). Nodes can be follower, candidate, or leader.
  - Time is logical via ticks; events drive state machine behavior. Deterministic outputs are required given the same initial state and event sequence.
  - Persistent state (hard state) must be durable before responding to RPCs that depend on it. Hard state includes current_term and voted_for, plus the log[] (and snapshot).
  - Elections: on randomised election timeouts, a follower may start a pre-vote phase, then a real election. A candidate becomes leader after receiving a majority of votes, after persisting hard state.
  - Voting rules: a node grants a vote if the term isn’t stale, it hasn’t voted for another candidate in that term, and the candidate’s log is at least as up-to-date as its own.
- Safety invariants ensured by the protocol:
  - Election Safety: at most one leader per term.
  - Leader Append-Only: leaders only append, never overwrite or delete entries in their own log.
  - Log Matching: if two logs share an entry with the same index and term, logs are identical up to that index.
  - Leader Completeness: any entry committed in a term appears in all later-term leaders.
  - State Machine Safety: once an entry at an index is applied by a node, no node will apply a different entry at that index.
- The document details how messages and state transitions operate to satisfy these properties, and marks the 1.0 surface as the stable contract for interoperability.

## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to manage a replicated log, offering a more understandable approach than Paxos while achieving equivalent results [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf). It focuses on strong leadership, randomized elections, and clear separation of concerns [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).

### Leader Election

Raft employs a randomized leader election process to quickly and cleanly resolve conflicts [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).

*   **Server States** A Raft cluster consists of servers that can be in one of four states: leader, candidate, follower, or learner [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md) [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
*   **Election Trigger** Elections are initiated by followers after a randomized timeout if they haven't received any communication (like AppendEntries or RequestVote RPCs) from a leader [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md) [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md). The minimum election timeout should be identical across servers [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md).
*   **Pre-Vote Phase** A follower may start a pre-vote phase before a real election [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
*   **Candidate Behavior** When a follower becomes a candidate, it requests votes from other nodes [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
*   **Voting Rules** A node grants a vote if its own term is not stale, it hasn't already voted for another candidate in the current term, and the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md). Before responding to RPCs that depend on it, a server must persist its hard state, including its current term and who it voted for [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
*   **Becoming Leader** A candidate becomes the leader after receiving a majority of votes [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
*   **Leader Authority** Once elected, the leader maintains its authority by sending periodic heartbeats to followers [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). It also commits a "no-op" entry at the start of its term [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md).
*   **Election Safety** The Raft protocol guarantees election safety, ensuring that at most one leader exists per term [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).

### Log Replication

In Raft, logs flow exclusively from the leader to followers, simplifying the replication process [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).

*   **Leader Responsibilities** The leader is responsible for accepting client commands, appending them to its log, replicating these entries to followers, and applying committed entries to its state machine [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md) [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
*   **AppendEntries RPCs** The leader replicates log entries to followers using AppendEntries RPCs [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). These RPCs include the leader's term, leader ID, the index and term of the log entry immediately preceding the new entries (PrevLogIndex/PrevLogTerm), the entries to append, and the leader's commit index (LeaderCommit) [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html). AppendEntries RPCs are idempotent and issued in parallel for efficiency [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md).
*   **Follower Log Consistency** When a follower receives an AppendEntries RPC:
    *   It rejects the request if the leader's term is older than its own current term [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
    *   It verifies that the `PrevLogIndex` and `PrevLogTerm` in the RPC match its own log to ensure consistency [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
    *   If there's a mismatch, the follower deletes conflicting entries and truncates its log from the point of mismatch onwards [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
    *   If the entries match, the follower appends the new entries [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
    *   It updates its term to the leader's term if necessary and responds with success [exokernel.github.io](https://exokernel.github.io/raft-deep-dive/log-replication/implementation-detail.html).
*   **Commitment Process** Log entries are considered committed when the leader has successfully replicated them to a majority of its followers [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). The leader tracks the highest known committed index and communicates it to followers via AppendEntries RPCs [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). Once an entry is committed, followers apply it to their state machines in log order [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md).
*   **Conflict Resolution and Recovery** If a follower's log lags behind or diverges from the leader's, the leader forces the follower's log to converge with its own by overwriting conflicting entries [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). If an AppendEntries RPC is rejected due to a log mismatch, the leader adjusts the `nextIndex` for that follower and retries until the logs align [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md). Leaders can retry failed AppendEntries indefinitely to ensure eventual consistency [github.com](https://github.com/databendlabs/openraft/blob/main/raft-essentials.md).
*   **Safety Invariants** Raft ensures several safety invariants related to log replication:
    *   **Leader Append-Only:** Leaders only append new entries to their logs; they never overwrite or delete existing entries [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
    *   **Log Matching:** If two logs contain an entry at the same index and with the same term, then their logs are identical up to that index [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
    *   **Leader Completeness:** Any log entry committed in a given term will appear in the logs of all subsequent leaders [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).
    *   **State Machine Safety:** Once an entry at a specific index is applied by a node to its state machine, no other node will apply a different entry at that same index [github.com](https://github.com/jamesgober/raft-io/blob/main/docs/PROTOCOL.md).

Summary:
- The document analyzes log replication in HashiCorp Raft implemented in Go, comparing it to a MIT 6.5840 class implementation.
- Leader behavior:
  - Leader appends new client commands to its log with term and command data.
  - Leader sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers, starting from each follower’s nextIndex. Each RPC contains: term, leaderId, PrevLogIndex/PrevLogTerm, Entries to append, and LeaderCommit.
  - Entries are sent asynchronously to followers when there are new entries to replicate.
- Follower behavior:
  - Follower rejects AppendEntries if the leader’s term is older than the follower’s current term.
  - Follower verifies that the preceding log entry (PrevLogIndex/PrevLogTerm) matches its own log to ensure consistency.
  - On mismatch, follower deletes conflicting entries and truncates its log beyond the point of mismatch.
  - If matching, follower appends new entries and advances its commitIndex to min(LeaderCommit, last new entry index) to avoid committing entries not yet received.
  - Follower responds with success and updates its term to the leader’s term as needed.
- Key correctness points highlighted include handling term comparisons, log prefix consistency, conflict resolution via truncation, and safe commit index advancement to maintain consistency with the leader.

- Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos while providing equivalent replicated state machine results.
- Key design features:
  - Strong leadership: a single leader pushes log entries to followers, simplifying log replication.
  - Randomized leader election: low-overhead timers resolve conflicts quickly.
  - Joint/multi-config membership changes: overlapping majorities ensure safety during cluster reconfigurations.
- Benefits highlighted:
  - Reduced state space and nondeterminism compared to Paxos, aiding understanding.
  - Empirical evidence from a user study: 43 students showed Raft understanding improves compared to Paxos.
  - On average, Raft quiz scores were higher: mean 25.7/60 for Raft vs 20.8/60 for Paxos (difference significant at 95% confidence; mean Raft score at least 2.5 points higher according to a paired t-test).

Here’s a concise synthesis of the essential results from the Raft overview:

- Purpose and guarantees
  - Raft provides a replicated log that leads to a replicated state machine: all followers execute the same commands in the same order.
  - A group of 2f+1 replicas tolerates f crashes; a majority is required to progress.
  - Safety: If a log entry is committed by the leader, it will appear in the logs of all future leaders (no overwriting of committed entries).

- Core concepts
  - Log entries: <index, term, command>, stored durably on disk; an entry is committed when it is known to be stored on a majority.
  - Leader role: The leader appends new commands to its log and sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers. Once committed, the leader applies the command to its state machine and informs the client (and piggybacks commitment to followers).
  - Follower role: Followers apply committed commands to their state machines and replicate the leader’s log.
  - Entry consistency: If two logs have the same index and term, they must have identical entries up to that point.

- Leader changes and safety
  - New leader’s log is considered truthful; no special recovery steps are required beyond normal operation.
  - Raft uses joint consensus during configuration changes to prevent conflicting majorities; final configuration changes are treated as log entries and replicated/committed like ordinary entries.
  - A leader is elected with a majority based on last-log-index/term; candidates include their last log index/term to maximize likelihood of containing committed entries.

- Election and liveness properties
  - Safety: at most one winner per term; each server votes once per term (votes persisted to stable storage).
  - Liveness: elections use randomized timeouts in [T, 2T], making it likely that one candidate wins before others start; works best when timeouts exceed typical network RTTs.

- Client interaction and reliability
  - Clients may be redirected to the leader if they contact a follower.
  - Exactly-once semantics are achieved by embedding a unique request ID in each command; leaders verify against duplicate IDs in their log, even across leader failures.

- Relation to other protocols
  - Raft resembles single-leader Paxos-style approaches (similar to multi-Paxos / viewstamped replication) but emphasizes clarity and implementability.
  - The log-driven approach ensures a simple, linearized path from log replication to state-machine updates.

If you want, I can tailor this to focus on specific aspects (e.g., safety proof sketch, leader election mechanics, or how configuration changes are handled).

Summary:

- The document outlines how Raft handles reads and writes across different peer states.
- Leader writes: updates include RequestConfigChange, Apply (log entry application to log and FSM), Barrier, LeadershipTransfer, Restore (Snapshot, excluding cluster config), and VerifyLeader (heartbeat to voters).
- Follower writes: BootstrapCluster initializes cluster configuration in local storage.
- Read operations: can be performed by any peer state. Key read-related commands include AppliedIndex, GetConfiguration, LastContact, LastIndex, Leader, Snapshot, State, and Stats.
- Run-time behavior: the main loop (run) branches by peer state (follower, candidate, leader) with specific RPC handling and internal actions:
  - Leader: handles replication to peers, applies a Noop log to commit up to the commit index, and processes various leader-specific channels (commit, verifyLeader, user restore snapshot, changeConfig, dispatchLogs).
  - Follower/Candidate: processes RPCs, including AppendEntries, RequestVote, InstallSnapshot, and other state-specific actions; candidates perform votes via askPeerForVote.
  - FSM and Snapshot: runFSM applies logs and restores snapshots; runSnapshot handles persisting snapshots and log compaction.
  - Snapshotting: periodic snapshotting for log compaction; user-triggered snapshots via userSnapshotCh.
  - Leadership transfer and config changes: managed via dedicated channels.
- Additional components: replicate (leader) manages sending Log Entry RPCs and heartbeat; pipelineDecode and heartbeat support ongoing replication and leader health checks.

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be simpler and safer than Paxos. It achieves agreement on a shared state machine across a cluster by electing a single leader responsible for log replication to followers; followers send heartbeats to the leader, and elections occur if heartbeats stop.

Key points:
- Safety guarantees: Election safety (at most one leader per term), leader append-only, log matching, leader completeness, and state machine safety.
- Leader-based operation: One leader handles client requests and replication; stability relies on timing and leader availability.
- Performance and scalability: Centralized leader creates a potential bottleneck and single point of failure; not inherently Byzantine fault-tolerant.
- Fault tolerance: Provides crash fault tolerance in its base form; Byzantine fault-tolerant variants exist but are not the default.
- Membership changes: Formal verification of the membership change process is lacking; there have been safety concerns and bugs in the past.
- Implementations: Widely implemented in Go, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Scala, with full specifications available.

Overall, Raft offers a verifiable, leader-based approach to replicating a state machine with strong safety properties, but it has known limitations in performance scaling, leader bottlenecks, and Byzantine fault tolerance.

runs.report:
## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to achieve consensus in distributed systems, providing a replicated log that leads to a replicated state machine, while being easier to understand and implement than Paxos [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/). Raft ensures that all non-failing servers in a cluster agree on the same sequence of commands (logs), producing identical state machine outputs [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/).

### Leader Election

Raft employs a strong leadership model where a single leader is responsible for managing log entries and replication [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).

*   **Process Overview:**
    *   Elections are triggered by randomized timeouts [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). This randomized approach helps to quickly resolve conflicts by making it likely that one candidate wins before others start, working best when timeouts exceed typical network round-trip times (RTTs) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Each server can be in one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   Followers send heartbeats to the leader [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). If a follower stops receiving heartbeats from the leader, it can transition to a candidate state and initiate an election [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
    *   When a server becomes a candidate, it increments its term, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote RPCs to other servers [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   Candidates include their last log index and term in their vote requests to maximize the likelihood of electing a leader that contains committed entries [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   A leader is elected when it receives votes from a majority of the servers in the cluster [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
    *   Each server votes only once per term, and these votes are persisted to stable storage to ensure safety [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Raft guarantees "Election Safety," meaning at most one leader can be elected per term [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).

*   **Leader Changes and Safety:**
    *   When a new leader is elected, its log is considered the truthful log, and no special recovery steps are required beyond normal operation [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   During configuration changes, Raft uses a "joint consensus" approach with overlapping majorities to prevent conflicting majorities and maintain safety [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). The final configuration changes are treated as log entries and are replicated and committed like ordinary entries [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

### Log Replication

Log replication in Raft is simplified by the strong leader model, where the leader pushes log entries to followers [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).

*   **Core Concepts:**
    *   Log entries consist of an index, a term, and a command [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). These entries are stored durably on disk [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   The leader appends new commands to its own log and then sends AppendEntries RPCs (Remote Procedure Calls) to its followers [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   Once a log entry is known to be stored on a majority of the servers, it is considered "committed" [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   After an entry is committed, the leader applies the command to its state machine and then informs the client [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). The leader also piggybacks commitment information to its followers via subsequent AppendEntries RPCs [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Followers apply committed commands to their state machines and replicate the leader's log [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Raft ensures "Log Matching," meaning if two logs have the same index and term, they must have identical entries up to that point [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
    *   The "Leader Completeness" property ensures that if a log entry is committed by a leader, it will appear in the logs of all future leaders, preventing committed entries from being overwritten [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).

*   **Operations and Safety Guarantees:**

## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to achieve consensus in distributed systems, providing a replicated log that leads to a replicated state machine, while being easier to understand and implement than Paxos [S1][S2][S4]. Raft ensures that all non-failing servers in a cluster agree on the same sequence of commands (logs), producing identical state machine outputs [S4].

### Leader Election

Raft employs a strong leadership model where a single leader is responsible for managing log entries and replication [S1][S5].

*   **Process Overview:**
    *   Elections are triggered by randomized timeouts [S1][S2]. This randomized approach helps to quickly resolve conflicts by making it likely that one candidate wins before others start, working best when timeouts exceed typical network round-trip times (RTTs) [S2].
    *   Each server can be in one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader [S3].
    *   Followers send heartbeats to the leader [S5]. If a follower stops receiving heartbeats from the leader, it can transition to a candidate state and initiate an election [S5].
    *   When a server becomes a candidate, it increments its term, votes for itself, and sends RequestVote RPCs to other servers [S3].
    *   Candidates include their last log index and term in their vote requests to maximize the likelihood of electing a leader that contains committed entries [S2].
    *   A leader is elected when it receives votes from a majority of the servers in the cluster [S2][S5].
    *   Each server votes only once per term, and these votes are persisted to stable storage to ensure safety [S2].
    *   Raft guarantees "Election Safety," meaning at most one leader can be elected per term [S5].

*   **Leader Changes and Safety:**
    *   When a new leader is elected, its log is considered the truthful log, and no special recovery steps are required beyond normal operation [S2].
    *   During configuration changes, Raft uses a "joint consensus" approach with overlapping majorities to prevent conflicting majorities and maintain safety [S1][S2]. The final configuration changes are treated as log entries and are replicated and committed like ordinary entries [S2].

### Log Replication

Log replication in Raft is simplified by the strong leader model, where the leader pushes log entries to followers [S1].

*   **Core Concepts:**
    *   Log entries consist of an index, a term, and a command [S2]. These entries are stored durably on disk [S2].
    *   The leader appends new commands to its own log and then sends AppendEntries RPCs (Remote Procedure Calls) to its followers [S2][S3].
    *   Once a log entry is known to be stored on a majority of the servers, it is considered "committed" [S2].
    *   After an entry is committed, the leader applies the command to its state machine and then informs the client [S2]. The leader also piggybacks commitment information to its followers via subsequent AppendEntries RPCs [S2].
    *   Followers apply committed commands to their state machines and replicate the leader's log [S2].
    *   Raft ensures "Log Matching," meaning if two logs have the same index and term, they must have identical entries up to that point [S2][S5].
    *   The "Leader Completeness" property ensures that if a log entry is committed by a leader, it will appear in the logs of all future leaders, preventing committed entries from being overwritten [S2][S5].

*   **Operations and Safety Guarantees:**
    *   The leader's writes include requests for configuration changes, applying log entries to the log and Finite State Machine (FSM), barrier operations, leadership transfer, restoring snapshots, and verifying the leader through heartbeats [S3].
    *   Followers initialize their cluster configuration in local storage via "BootstrapCluster" [S3].
    *   Raft tolerates `f` crashes in a group of `2f+1` replicas, as a majority is always required to make progress [S2].
    *   Periodic snapshotting is used for log compaction, and users can also trigger snapshots [S3]. The `runSnapshot` component handles persisting snapshots [S3].

  - Leader role: The leader appends new commands to its log and sends AppendEntries RPCs to followers. Once committed, the leader applies the command to its state machine and informs the client (and piggybacks commitment to followers).
  - Follower role: Followers apply committed commands to their state machines and replicate the leader’s log.
  - Entry consistency: If two logs have the same index and term, they must have identical entries up to that point.

- Leader changes and safety
  - New leader’s log is considered truthful; no special recovery steps are required beyond normal operation.
  - Raft uses joint consensus during configuration changes to prevent conflicting majorities; final configuration changes are treated as log entries and replicated/committed like ordinary entries.
  - A leader is elected with a majority based on last-log-index/term; candidates include their last log index/term to maximize likelihood of containing committed entries.

- Election and liveness properties
  - Safety: at most one winner per term; each server votes once per term (votes persisted to stable storage).
  - Liveness: elections use randomized timeouts in [T, 2T], making it likely that one candidate wins before others start; works best when timeouts exceed typical network RTTs.

- Client interaction and reliability
  - Clients may be redirected to the leader if they contact a follower.
  - Exactly-once semantics are achieved by embedding a unique request ID in each command; leaders verify against duplicate IDs in their log, even across leader failures.

  - Raft resembles single-leader Paxos-style approaches (similar to multi-Paxos / viewstamped replication) but emphasizes clarity and implementability.

- Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos while providing equivalent replicated state machine results.
- Key design features:
  - Strong leadership: a single leader pushes log entries to followers, simplifying log replication.
  - Randomized leader election: low-overhead timers resolve conflicts quickly.
  - Joint/multi-config membership changes: overlapping majorities ensure safety during cluster reconfigurations.
- Benefits highlighted:
  - Reduced state space and nondeterminism compared to Paxos, aiding understanding.
  - Empirical evidence from a user study: 43 students showed Raft understanding improves compared to Paxos.
  - On average, Raft quiz scores were higher: mean 25.7/60 for Raft vs 20.8/60 for Paxos (difference significant at 95% confidence; mean Raft score at least 2.5 points higher according to a paired t-test).
- Practical emphasis: Raft’s structure supports building practical systems and provides a clear foundation for implementation, including handling basic, corner-case, and reconfiguration scenarios.

Summary of essential results:

- Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be as effective as Paxos but easier to understand. It achieves equivalent replicated-state-machine results with a simpler structure and clearer separation of concerns (leader election, log replication, safety).
- Key innovations that improve understandability and practicality:
  - Strong leader: one leader manages log entries to followers, simplifying replication.
  - Leader election: randomized timers resolve conflicts quickly with minimal extra mechanism.
  - Membership changes: a joint-consensus approach with overlapping majorities maintains safety during configuration changes.
- Usability study: 43 students compared Raft to Paxos. Results show Raft is significantly easier to understand:
  - On Raft vs Paxos quizzes, 33 out of 43 participants scored higher on the Raft quiz.
  - Mean scores: Raft ≈ 25.7 / 60 vs Paxos ≈ 20.8 / 60.
  - Statistical analysis (paired t-test) indicates Raft scores are higher with confidence; a linear model also links scores to quiz type and prior Paxos experience.
- Overall claim: Raft provides the same safety and correctness guarantees as Paxos while offering a clearer design and better learning outcomes, with practical mechanisms for leader management and dynamic membership.

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be simpler and safer than Paxos. It achieves agreement on a shared state machine across a cluster by electing a single leader responsible for log replication to followers; followers send heartbeats to the leader, and elections occur if heartbeats stop.

Key points:
- Safety guarantees: Election safety (at most one leader per term), leader append-only, log matching, leader completeness, and state machine safety.
- Leader-based operation: One leader handles client requests and replication; stability relies on timing and leader availability.
- Performance and scalability: Centralized leader creates a potential bottleneck and single point of failure; not inherently Byzantine fault-tolerant.
- Fault tolerance: Provides crash fault tolerance in its base form; Byzantine fault-tolerant variants exist but are not the default.
- Membership changes: Formal verification of the membership change process is lacking; there have been safety concerns and bugs in the past.
- Implementations: Widely implemented in Go, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Scala, with full specifications available.

Overall, Raft offers a verifiable, leader-based approach to replicating a state machine with strong safety properties, but it has known limitations in performance scaling, leader bottlenecks, and Byzantine fault tolerance.

- The document outlines how Raft handles reads and writes across different peer states.
- Leader writes: updates include RequestConfigChange, Apply (log entry application to log and FSM), Barrier, LeadershipTransfer, Restore (Snapshot, excluding cluster config), and VerifyLeader (heartbeat to voters).
- Follower writes: BootstrapCluster initializes cluster configuration in local storage.
- Read operations: can be performed by any peer state. Key read-related commands include AppliedIndex, GetConfiguration, LastContact, LastIndex, Leader, Snapshot, State, and Stats.
- Run-time behavior: the main loop (run) branches by peer state (follower, candidate, leader) with specific RPC handling and internal actions:
  - Leader: handles replication to peers, applies a Noop log to commit up to the commit index, and processes various leader-specific channels (commit, verifyLeader, user restore snapshot, changeConfig, dispatchLogs).
  - Follower/Candidate: processes RPCs, including AppendEntries, RequestVote, InstallSnapshot, and other state-specific actions; candidates perform votes via askPeerForVote.
  - FSM and Snapshot: runFSM applies logs and restores snapshots; runSnapshot handles persisting snapshots and log compaction.
  - Snapshotting: periodic snapshotting for log compaction; user-triggered snapshots via userSnapshotCh.
  - Leadership transfer and config changes: managed via dedicated channels.
- Additional components: replicate (leader) manages sending Log Entry RPCs and heartbeat; pipelineDecode and heartbeat support ongoing replication and leader health checks.
